story_text.value:
Hey we are Housecat.

I've spend the last 15 years building dev tools at Heroku, Convox (YC S15), and Segment. Dev tools have gotten insanely good over the decades, now we're working to level up productivity tools for everyday work.

Housecat is an email inbox running on an single-tenant agent computer with a durable workflow engine and connections to common tools for day-to-day work.

My primary workflow with the product is for customer support: get a support email, trigger a triage process, open a GitHub issue, spin up a coding agent to fix it, and update the customer along the way. All from the same UI and sandbox.

We've experimented with lots of different approaches to new workspace tools, and learned that many people still need a great GUI. We've landed on the email inbox as a very familiar and permanent surface and are building tools and automations directly inside it.

Under the hood every user gets their own single-tenant sandbox VM and persistent SSD on exe.dev.

User connections to Google, Slack, GitHub, etc. are managed in an external service so the VM and agent are subject to external governance and don’t have direct access to secrets.

Durable workflows are built on DBOS.dev. Running interactive and deterministic workflows directly inside an email couldn’t feel more different than chatting about emails in Claude.app.

The app is built on HTMX, Unix, Go, and SQLite. The app is source available to users and the Linux VM is fully open for a user and their agent to poke around.

You can try it out at https://home.housecat.com/beta. It requires a Google / Gmail connection for the email app, which you can revoke any time.

We'd love to share more and learn how the community here is managing email, agentic chat, and custom workflows for their work.

story_text.value:
HN is great for the links people share, but a big part of the value I get comes from reading the discussion around them. I realized I was always opening the article in one tab and the comments in another, constantly switching back and forth.

I figured there was probably a simpler way, so I threw together this userscript to merge the two.

1. Clicking a link from Hacker News opens the article with a side panel containing the discussion. It doesn't require your credentials, is resizable, and is easy to tweak if you want to customize it.

2. If you land on an article that has previously been shared on HN, the script finds the existing discussion and adds a button in the top-right to open the panel.

Feedback welcome.

Hi HN, I'm Josh. WallHop is a free paywall bypass: paste an article URL (or prefix any URL with wallhop.io/) and you get the readable article without the paywall popup, ads or clutter. No signup, no extension.

I built it after 12ft.io went away. The News Media Alliance took it down in July 2025 and I missed having something I could hit from my phone.

How it works: it started as a fork of everywall/ladder (GPL-3.0) and I've modified it heavily since. Instead of relying on one trick, it chains several bypass methods per request and falls back to archive.is when they all fail, so one site blocking one technique doesn't break it.

Things that might be interesting:

- iOS Shortcut: on iPhone, tap Share > WallHop from any article in Safari or another app. This is how I use it 95% of the time. - It works on Medium member-only posts, which 12ft never handled. - Bookmarklet for desktop, plus /raw/<url> and /api/<url> endpoints if you want to script it.

I've tested it against most major news outlets and a bunch of local papers. It won't work everywhere. There are SOME server-side paywalls that are out of reach, and I'd rather say that up front. If you find a site that breaks, I'd love the link, and I can likely figure out a way to bypass it!

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 (https://agent37.com). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox.

You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo

We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses.

One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings.

Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month.

Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost:

* When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost.

* Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost.

* Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators.

* And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host.

We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques.

Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff.

I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya.

If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform.

Thanks!

https://agent37.com

story_text.value:
Back when I lived in Central Florida, it took me years to learn what native plants could benefit wildlife and the local ecosystem as I slowly replaced parts of my yard to make it more resilient to drought. After moving to Seattle a few years ago, I had to start all of that from scratch. LLMs made the process a bit easier but I still had to routinely ask the same kinds of questions over and over, despite being far more familiar with native plants these days and leaning more on native plant societies and botany resources like Doug Tallamy and Joey Santore whose excellent Crime Pays But Botany Doesn't site was recently posted here[1].

A good friend was visiting from Orlando over the summer and told me she was struggling to decide what to plant in her own yard despite her landlord being ok with it. That was enough of an excuse for me to kick off work on Indigene, which is aimed at giving folks just-in-time knowledge about what to plant based on their locale, sun exposure, soil conditions, and their own ecosystem support goals.

Candidly, as many of us have, I've also leaned heavily on LLMs (mostly Claude here) to bring this to life. Largely to avoid saying demonstrably false things, which might be an absurd statement. You can find the GitHub repository[2] a wild array of open data sources I've dug out and cross-referenced to ensure mistakes and hallucinations are unlikely to survive for long. But given today's Indigenous Peoples Day I figured it was past time I shared the projects and invited more scrutiny.

Being the Keep a Changelog guy, you can bet it has extensive release notes[3] generated from the project changelog. Those are also parsed into feature-specific guides so each also lists relevant recent updates.

Lastly, I put together a post[5] that goes into a bit more detail on the story of the project and what I've learned along the way.

I really, really hope people here (and beyond) find it as useful and enlightening as I do.

PS: before it comes up, all the LLM usage for the project is documented[6] and used as warning system in every PR but I think there's a lot more I can do to further reduce it

story_text.value:
So I've been working on a project (Make0 AI) for a long time where I wanted to give common context to both Codex and Claude Code. The problem is simple - while working on Claude and after exhausting the daily/weekly limits I've start again from scratch in Codex. Of course I can prompt Claude to summarise a handoff that I can give to Codex but that is inefficient. So I thought of a creating a common context for both of them locally using a simple list of instructions like a shared md file. But the problem was the file kept on growing and after some point the common context went beyond 20k tokens and was just inflating the token budget unnecessarily.

Then I implemented a RAG based retrieval approach on the list to only load what is required for that prompt and voila, after a few more iterations it resulted into a graph memory - Brain.

So this product Make0 AI gives you the ability to create Brains that you can connect to any Ai agent via MCP and then they immediately know your likes, dislikes, preferences etc. AI agents can read, write to this memory.

This can be your long term memory and the agents just become the token providers and task executors. You have full control over your data/memories from a single place. Think of this as a "USB thumb drive brain" that you plug to any agent.

I know I may not be the first one to implement this but I tried to make the UX simple and is not at all developer focused. You can just drag and drop your memories/data to the brain and even play around with a visual brain.

One more thing, i've done benchmarks on the memory. LoCoMo scores 83.3% overall, with Single hop 92.5% in standard mode (available now) and in another configuration (experimental max mode) it scores 92% overall and 94.4% in single hop. Available in the benchmark page. It uses hybrid search + graph memory and has built in conflict resolution for memories.

Do let me know if you folks wanna try it!

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I've been through many finance tracking apps, starting with Personal Capital, then Monarch, and most recently Copilot. None of them have worked perfectly for my needs.

All of these apps tend to model “cash flow” as the net sum of your transactions during a month, yet while credit card charges are reported immediately, they are typically deducted from checking (cash) accounts the following month when the bill is due. As a result, I've always had to maintain a separate spreadsheet to track my actual cash flow.

These apps also have a huge focus on managing budgets, which has never been for me. My spending is rarely consistent month-to-month, so every month I'm comparing my fully justified spending against my budget, and tweaking my budget until I “pass”.

So I built yet another finance tracking app. It has the usual components - accounts, transactions, categories - but the core is a cash flow projection engine, and everything else is built around it.

Budgets are gone. Instead, each income/spending category is projected forward from your historical activity, but not as a flat monthly number. They land in whatever account you historically use (e.g. checking account for paychecks/rent/bills, credit/debit cards for daily spending). Credit card payments are modeled automatically based on your projected credit card balance. You can set up your own recurring transfers between accounts as well, to model savings, for example.

The end result is that the app can forecast how your cash moves, and you can see in advance when any account might run low. If all of your accounts look good for the next 12 months, maybe you don't have a budgeting problem.

What’s made the biggest difference for me has been the MCP integration, which I have connected to Claude (but can be connected to any AI agent of your choice). I have asked it to import historical transactions by uploading PDF account statements, categorize/tag all transactions that took place while I was on vacation, and plan transfers across my accounts to cover expected payments.

I hope some people that share my frustrations will find this app useful.

story_text.value:
Inspired by the discussion in [1], I have an adjacent question: did your team organization and work methods change?

In our company we still try to play by the (old) book: backlogs, estimates, iterations, feature teams, PR reviews, etc., but the entire thing leaks everywhere you look. There is no point in many of the old rituals, but it is also not clear how to organize ourselves now. This is different, albeit closely related, from the question of how to adjust as an IC.

For example:

- In our team, we almost don't see the point in PR reviews anymore, not in the old way anyway. Generated code is always good enough, and in a sense is already reviewed once by the developer who signed off (the topic is discussed in [1]). So, we are now thinking to abandon PRs, or change what we review and how we do it. We are adding more rules for code review agents and to CI. We are also thinking to replace code reviews by "concept reviews" or similar.

- Speaking of those, we still try to find the right place and a process for architecture and specifications reviews. They seem to become a new subject of PR reviews in fact, but we are not there yet.

- In many places we don't see the need to share the workload and knowledge between multiple developers. Reverting to the model where one developer is responsible for an entire component seems viable again. Although we are naturally worried about BusFactor=1.

- Some Agile-inspired practices still work for us, namely iterative development and "deploy when ready". But the development process itself starts to resemble the old-school waterfall-ish one: think everything through, write down your constraints and your specs, design the architecture first, then (re)generate the code at will. I wonder what other practices will go away or get adopted.

There are probably more examples, hopefully you get the gist. I am very interested in discussing how do we organize the teams now? What did you try? What works, what doesn't?

[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50151036 (Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?)

story_text.value:
Hey HN, this is Andy from Respan (https://www.respan.ai). We are building an open-source Rust AI gateway. It is a decoupled gateway, so everything is a plugin, including different providers, protocols (MCP, voice), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features (fallbacks, PII redaction, smart routing).

Instead of packaging tons of providers and features into one gateway, Respan provides a small core and public interfaces that teams can use to assemble the AI infrastructure their application needs. That way, users can build their own features as additional plugins without having to change the gateway's core.

Here’s a video demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVv2ibXiTXM

There are countless LLM gateways and most of them solve a common problem: calling different providers from a single endpoint. However, adding new features can become prohibitively difficult. So developers can end up building another gateway to solve a specific problem.

We've been building our gateway based on LiteLLM since 2024, and now it's providing services for thousands of orgs. Each org needs different API key settings, routes, and limits. To support that, we kept wrapping LiteLLM, adding more features to it, and at one stage, our wrapper code exceeded 100,000 lines.

This January, a routine LiteLLM upgrade caused intermittent connection errors, and we had to roll back. We still haven't figured out the cause, but since then, we no longer upgrade LiteLLM directly and instead manually backport upstream fixes. These experiences made us realize that continuing to patch LiteLLM is not a sustainable long-term solution, and we had to redesign the gateway ourselves.

While redesigning our gateway, we wanted to make it easier to add features without breaking existing ones. Inspired by Nginx, we think an AI gateway should have a really small core, only responsible for dispatching events.

We believe that everything should be a plugin in our gateway, including providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini), protocols (chat, realtime voice, MCP), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features for reliability and security (smart routing, fallbacks, and PII redaction through example plugins). Beyond that, we want developers to be able to easily extend the gateway's capabilities by adding their own plugins, without touching the core. Adding a provider, even your own, is dead simple, because quirks are plugins too and there’s nothing magical about them. A provider is a short file, Mistral’s is 22 lines, and each quirk, like Groq putting token usage in its own field, gets its own test.

Respan Gateway does more than let you call Claude or Gemini models from the OpenAI SDK. It handles tools, images, and reasoning protocols automatically: an application based on the OpenAI Realtime API can also use Gemini Live through the gateway, though not every feature translates. A simple chat app can use MCP tools configured in the gateway, without implementing MCP itself.

We also parse requests into a shared structure. When the client and provider use the same API, we preserve provider-specific fields in their native format, even if our shared structure doesn't have a field for them. That way, the gateway can write them back instead of dropping them.

Here’s how it works:

An adapter hands each HTTP or WebSocket connection to the first client format that recognizes it. The format exposes the request as a two-way stream of typed input and output events. The core runs plugins in registration order, allowing them to choose a provider, filter or wrap either stream, make additional calls, return a response, or refuse the request. A provider format then opens the upstream connection.

If the client and provider use the same format and no plugin changes the payload, the original bytes and protocol-specific fields can pass through unchanged. When formats differ, they translate through shared types for messages, tool calls, results, streams, and usage. This stream model can represent both one-shot HTTP requests and long-lived bidirectional sessions.

The gateway is open source at https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway under the MIT or Apache-2.0 license. You don't need to use Respan's hosted platform and can run it directly on your local machine. Build it from source, add your provider keys, and swap the base URL in a supported client. You can keep using the API your client already speaks. It's still pre-alpha.

We make money from our hosted platform (https://www.respan.ai/pricing), which runs the gateway for you with native observability and evals, along with unified billing.

If you’re building routing, tools, filtering, observability, or security for agents, we'd love to see it as a plugin. PLUGINS.md in the repo explains how to write one and links to the plugins we’ve created so far. Turning that into an ecosystem is basically our roadmap, and we welcome you to contribute your own plugins. We'd love to answer any questions and hear your feedback!

https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway

I have noticed that a lot of job posts that do not use any ATS, and in order to apply, they put their emails and ask candidates to apply with “X” in email subject. That seemed to be very counter productive — imagine having 300+ emails with resumes. Where do you manage them? In Excel? Or how many good candidates you never get to.

I researched popular ATS systems and found out that they require yearly / monthly subscriptions. A lot of them do not have a pricing on the website, so you gotta book a call to be quoted some yearly contract price…

So I built Worklicant — lightweight ATS for tech hiring.

Pay per vacancy. Post a job, share the link, easy application form (no registration needed for applicants). Easy in-app scheduling. Vacancy analytics. Custom hiring stages, tags, notes, application questions.

AI extraction of resume summary, companies, experiences so you do not have to open each resume. You can also write a rejection prompt with ideal candidate description. That will be taken into account when AI (Jev) gives score to each applicant.

I have worked on it for around 2 years on and off so most of the code was hand written (but that’s changing rapidly).

Give it a try and let me know what you think!

story_text.value:
Hi HN! We’re Srikar and Kevan, founders of Alter – https://alterauth.com/. We’re building access control for agents that can take actions on behalf of multiple users.

If you’ve built an internal agent people use through Slack, you may have experienced this scenario: everyone signs in with their own account, but the agent connects to the CRM or billing system with one shared API key, so the agent can do anything that the key can do. User-level authentication in Slack does nothing to control what the agent can do in an external system like the CRM or billing system.

Here’s what Alter does:

-It acts as a proxy and manages downstream credentials for every API request that an agent takes;

-It takes identity into account for every action the agent does. Automatically take into account the end user identity of the person that the agent is taking actions on behalf of.

-It enforces fine grained runtime policies and records compliance grade audit logs.

Here’s a demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ZqPU14ipGE

We started this because we saw first hand how hard it is to build agents in regulated industries. To unlock the true benefits of agents we need to allow agents to take actions, sometimes actions on behalf of end users. I (Srikar) was working at Goldmans and I saw how prohibitively expensive it was for me as a developer to write my own custom auth to enable multi-tenancy in agents and to allow agents to have strict policy controls as they act on behalf of end users. My co-founder, Kevan, is a second time founder and was previously working on a database startup. He has experience building and selling deep tech into highly regulated environments. So this problem seemed like a natural fit for the both of us.

Building and maintaining custom auth for multi tenant agents was challenging. But so was ensuring that the solution we developed was secure, scalable and keeping track of security grade audit logs. As a result we realized there needs to be a separate product category for this that enables developers to easily build secure multi user agents that can actually take actions in an enterprise. Some of the real-world use cases we’ve seen include:

We have built a multi user open claw for our own team using Alter that saved us countless hours on our GTM effort. Link here:https://github.com/AlterAIDev/openclaw-alter-plugin

We have multiple startups who have used our platform to build their own secure internal agents for everything ranging from SRE agents to back office agents dealing with Quickbooks and payroll platforms like Rippling. It has saved developers countless hours both in terms of building and maintenance. We also have a defense contractor building air gapped agents for marine corp using Alter.

Under the hood, the value that we provide is that we do a lot of the plumbing that no one wants to do. We support hundreds of providers, all manually tested end to end. Reliability is our biggest priority. We have built this in a way to allow developers to custom build their agents however they see fit. Everything ranging from custom policies, agent delegation, user attribution, audit logs needed for compliance to a LLM gateway with guardrails (Coming soon)

Building a security product is hard. We have learnt that in order to build a truly secure product, security thinking has to pervade every part of the development process. We have embraced shift left security. Every PR that is pushed out is continuously checked for supply chain attacks, potentially dangerous code patterns etc.

Our business plan revolved around usage based pricing. There is a free tier up to 10k requests and then a pricing tier starting beyond that. We would love it if people configured their APIs and OAuth credentials, tried out the policies and actually built agents that can take actions with alter!

If you’ve built an agent that acts for multiple users, how are you handling permissions today? We’d especially like to hear what you’ve had to build yourself.

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

Loudwalk (https://loudwalk.com/?from=hn) is an app I built for myself to review my Anki flashcards out loud on a walk, and am excited to share today.

Anki has changed my life and is probably the best habit I've managed to stick with. Apart from helping at my tech day-job and remembering random things I find interesting (relatives' birthdays, quotes, poetry), it allowed me to become conversational in Russian in 2 years and complete the first year of a French university degree in Art History - all while working full-time as CTO and co-founder at my company. I have an average memory at best, and it is crazy what Anki unlocks with consistency.

Recently I've been exploring how interacting with LLMs by voice can help me spend less time at a screen and more time active and outdoors, for two main reasons:

- wanting to be more active/healthy as I'm in my mid-thirties and starting to get back pain

- just had a newborn and spend a lot of time carrying him or doing chores around the house

Most of my time sitting at my desk is spent waiting for coding agents and reviewing Anki cards. After building Notiferry (https://notiferry.com/) to forward macOS notifications to my iPhone, the next obvious move was Loudwalk: an LLM asks your card questions, listens to your spoken answer, and grades it. Voice reviews give a cadence I don't have on screen, cutting my daily review time in half (from 90 minutes to 45), and walking while reviewing helps both memorization and mood. Time simply doesn't have the same flavor staring at a monitor vs walking in nature or holding your baby.

What Loudwalk does:

- Import your decks with full history and media from Anki (and export back to Anki with no lock-in; includes a starter deck and CSV import if you don't use Anki yet)

- Start a voice review from any deck (works with Siri so your phone stays in your pocket)

- Spoken grading + "deep dives": if you stumble on a card or want context, ask out loud to start a live conversation on the subject, with live web fact-checking when dates or connections matter. Say "next" to return to your queue

- Question rewording: rephrases questions so you memorize the concept, not the exact card wording

- Phonetic grading + deterministic timing: on-device STT mangles proper nouns, so the LLM grades phonetically/semantically against your card's answer, while response-time caps (Again/Hard/Good/Easy) are applied deterministically in code

- On-device speech recognition; grading and deep dives use OpenAI models (a mix of GPT-6 Luna and Sol + GPT-Live-1)

It runs on iPhone (iOS 26) and Apple silicon Mac (macOS 26). No Android or Windows.

I haven't planned to open-source it for now as I'm seeing if it can support me working on it long-term. Visual reviews (Anki-style) are free forever; voice reviews require a subscription ($9.99/mo) after a 7-day trial (no account or credit card required). Sync across Mac and iPhone uses append-only JSONL review logs in your own iCloud Drive - no server in the sync path, and visual reviews + sync + export work offline forever.

I switched to Loudwalk over 3 months ago (>3k spoken reviews) with first-class support for English and French, plus a CLI so coding agents can add cards at the end of a study session.

Happy to answer any questions about the app or spaced repetition!

story_text.value:
reVault is a new, secure-by-default archive format called a lockbox, designed to be simple to use.

I've been working on reVault for about 2 years. It was originally written in Dart, but with the improvements in AI, I decided to port it to Rust using AI.

It's now in beta, so I'm looking for feedback, particularly around the different language bindings.

A lockbox is encrypted, signed and compressed by default. Each can be disabled selectively.

  - Hybrid post-quantum or passphrase encryption, including metadata.
  - Zstd compression.
  - Pure Rust libraries wherever possible.
We intend to phase out remaining C code as alternatives become available. The project has been scanned using OpenAI's Daybreak cyber security tools.

The manual is a work in progress: https://docs.revault.onepub.dev/

reVault supports Linux, macOS and Windows, x64 and arm64, plus Wasm. The core is Rust, with bindings for C/C++, Java, Dart, Python, Ruby, JS/TypeScript, Go, C#, Kotlin, Lua, PHP and Swift.

Within a lockbox you can store:

  - Files, directories, permissions and symlinks.
  - Variables.
  - Forms.
Variables, forms and the lockbox itself can have descriptions.

reVault uses a portable vault (just another lockbox with structured content) to hold your keys, contacts' keys, lockbox aliases and form definitions.

It ties into your platform's secure store, so logging into your desktop unlocks your vault. You don't have to enter a passphrase every time you access a lockbox. You can disable this.

There are lots of shortcuts. Creating a lockbox stores an alias in your vault, based on its filename or a name you choose:

  lbx create /some/path/mybox.lbox
  lbx mybox open --duration 1h
  lbx mybox var set KEY VALUE
Set a default lockbox and you can leave its name out:

  lbx session default mybox
  lbx var get KEY
You can mirror a directory tree into a lockbox and update it when the directory changes:

  lbx store.lbox mirrors project create --from ./project --to /projects/project
  lbx store.lbox mirrors update
The API lets you read, write and seek within files without extracting them to the filesystem. Each lockbox has a table of contents, so extracting a single file from a multi-gigabyte lockbox is fast.

Recovery

Updates are transactional, with automatic rollback for failed updates. The format is designed for recovery: content is stored in pages, allowing unaffected content to be recovered if part of a lockbox is corrupted.

Sharing

An encrypted lockbox is more useful if you can share it.

reVault has an open-source keyserver for exchanging public keys, with validation through a second trusted channel. It's still experimental.

OnePub has donated a server to run a single keyserver. If you're interested in donating resources, I'd like to bring up a second redundant server. It's pure Rust, uses under 100 MB RSS and supports rate limits.

To publish your default profile's public key:

  lbx vault profiles email you@example.com
  lbx vault profiles publish
Give the publish code to your contact. They can import your key:

  lbx vault contacts receive <publish-code> <contact-name>
Display your profile's fingerprint and exchange it through a second trusted channel:

  lbx vault profiles fingerprint
Repeat the process in the opposite direction to get their key. Once you have it, grant them access to your default lockbox:

  lbx access grant alice
You can then email the encrypted lockbox to Alice.

To install the CLI and get started:

  cargo install revault_cli
  lbx vault init
  lbx completion install
Completion installation detects your shell. To diagnose issues:

  lbx doctor
The language bindings are published to their respective package repositories.

I'm looking for constructive criticism of the project on its own merits, particularly the APIs and language bindings. I'm not interested in a debate about using AI.

When GPT-6/Gemini launched recently, a lot of the 3D demos used blender-mcp (https://github.com/ahujasid/blender-mcp). It's cool, but you have to install blender locally and wire up plugins just to try a prompt or share a run.

I built a browser-based 3D mesh playground so you can hook up your own coding agent over MCP (or run in-browser) directly in a tab. It runs on three.js + manifold-3d for blender-like boolean/mesh editing in JS, and gives the agent a render_preview tool to take multi-view screenshots (front/right/top/iso + custom camera angles + clay mode). That way the agent can look at what it built and fix the geometry, similar to how it iterates when building a website.

The submitted link is a trace of Gemini reconstructing a Copenhagen canal scene from a photo: it hits a script error on the first pass, fixes the bug, and then goes through several rounds of checking 4-view and close-up render_preview screenshots to tweak the geometry.

story_text.value:
Hi, I want to share with you my chrome extension: Tabverse, as it is now passed the reveiw of Chrome Web Store and live at: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/tabverse/lffblcippn...

Tabverse is a local first workona like chrome extension for managing tabs, with its source open at https://www.github.com/liyu1981/tabverse.

In essential it has the core functions workona has, but can operate totally locally, which means it will not need an account nor subscription. The only limit is your local storage spaces so that you can have as many spaces(I call tabverse) as you can. It is open source, so not just your data stays with you, and the tool itself will stay with you in future.

Beyond the normal workona features (persisted workspace, load/reload/import/export, note/bookmark/history tools), there are features does require a server. Features like backup/sync, global search on all tabverses, and future collaboration (not yet done), can only be possible if there is a server. I build this part in open too: the server is free to self host and open source in same repo of Tabverse.

The tabverse's idea was with me few years ago while I was using Workona and was frustrated with its limitation on free tier (remember was only 5 workspaces), and the missing features of managing multiple workspaces at the same time. Tabverse takes the idea of Workona, and develop further: each window with a Tabverse tab is a workspace, all stored in local storage, and multi windows can have multi Tabverses same time, and can switch fast. There can even be window without Tabverse, so besides work, personal stuff or entertainment will have place to go. As I build this alone, in the middle, almost give up on this project, and luckily AI agents now is there: not only I have a good helper, but also I have a partner I can discuss a bit. So this time the first version starts with v0.7.2.

But AI agent can never replace the real need from human on what should be built and what works better, so I want to share with you and listen to your feedbacks early. Please give it a try, and every feedback to me is a gift.

Besides the self-hosted option, I host a server at https://tabverse.liyu1981.xyz (yes, the same website of intro and docs), but is invitation only. If you want to help me to test in this early stage, you can login with Google (the only social login I configured :)), and request an invitation there. I will act as soon as I find your request :). But do not worry at all if you only want to use Tabverse locally without a server -- that is the first thing when I was building it.

In current version there are also AI features built in, and again do not worry as the AI features is using Chrome's Prompt API, which is totally local, with Gemini Nano (first time will need to download it automatically), nothing send to a server, and you can always turn this on of off in settings. Morden computers with decent memory should work well, but some older computer may suffer (so please turn off). And it is Chrome only. (Honestly, Tabverse currently only support Google Chrome, but not other Chrome based browsers).

For the busy people out there, the GitHub repo has a demo video so you can see if this is worth your time: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

The video was created by Opus 5.5; I just asked it to create a demo video (it has a 'record' tool), so I think this is a good idea of how well it can work with the tool.

---

pw-repl is a tool that makes it easy for you and your agents to work with Playwright+CDP in a browser (your current headed session, or a headless one, or both at the same time; take your pick).

It's basically a Playwright-powered swiss army knife that helps you and agents poke around your browser: Try out different features of a website, break things (e.g. mock backend responses), take screenshots, record videos, etc.

The GitHub repo shows a video, recorded by an agent using pw-repl: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

One cool thing it can do: create videos of bug reports. You can tell an agent about a bug and to use pw-repl to capture it, and it can record a video with the built-in toast feature to narrate its actions, and show a virtual mouse to simulate actions on the screen, as if it were a user. It's also useful for capturing screenshots (which can be combined with the toast and highlight tools to emphasize certain elements or information), and has many useful features that can help agents to use it efficiently.

This isn't intended to be commercialized in any way. It's just a neat tool that I (with Claude's help) cobbled together. It's completely vibe-coded, and is intended mainly as a debugging aid. I use all the time, and hope it may be helpful for others.

It's basically just Playwright + CDP under the hood, but has some extra tools and an interface that make it easier for agents to work with.

The quickest way to try it out is to tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background --launch`, which starts a headless Chromium of its own. No browser setup needed. (If you don't like such `curl | bash`-esque installation instructions, read the code, or get your agent to take a look at it.)

To use it in your own browser instead, start Chrome with CDP enabled (`chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir="$HOME/.config/chrome-debug"`), and tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background`. (The separate `--user-data-dir` is needed because recent versions of Chrome don't open the debugging port on your default profile.)

It also can generate a skill so that you can just run `/pw-repl do some stuff`. Get your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest skill > <skills folder>/pw-repl/SKILL.md` (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/pw-repl/SKILL.md` for Claude Code).

NOTE: This has only been tested on my Linux machine, so not sure if it will work on macOS. It should, but I haven't tried it out personally.

Fun fact: This tool was originally a random REPL that Claude generated on-the-fly to do some random thing. I saw it and was blown away, so I got Claude to make it into its own application. I suspect that Claude may have taken "inspiration" from an existing project with a similar name, so credit where credit is due to this other `playwright-repl` package: https://github.com/stevez/playwright-repl

story_text.value:
At Researchly (https://www.researchly.at) we automate market and competitive analysis. We learned that on-the-fly web search through AI agents isn't reliable enough for consistent, in-depth work.

Existing data providers such as PitchBook or Crunchbase are either too expensive or lack the data we need: operational signals such as management changes or new partnerships, for DACH. Furthermore, search tools such as Exa tend to be probabilistic. What they return depends on the model and on SEO rankings, so two runs of the same query can give you two different answers.

So we built our own search layer: several providers (Exa, Linkup, Tavily, Parallel), allow/deny lists, source rankings (we once caught ourselves citing our own blog posts), and checks whether an empty result means "nothing there" or "out of budget".

It works, but: it's slow, expensive, non-deterministic & we kept redoing the same research for different clients (which makes it very un-economic).

So we started building the data layer itself. Step one was Firmendaten (300k companies from the Austrian register; shared here last week https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50142669).

Relational data like that is already a huge improvement, but what we really need is a graph, as people ask "W" questions: who does what with whom where and when. This is our first attempt at it.

For now, it just connects who partners with whom and company groups. (Tick "Beziehungen 2. Ebene" to see every partner and person)

It's small (a few dozen robotics companies) but you can already see how complex the graph gets & it serves as a good PoC for us.

We had wanted to build this for a long time, and it turned out to be far harder than we expected. One thing that sounds trivial but was particularly hard: finding the right website for a company.

You can buy that data. There are enrichment APIs that return a company's website. But even if they cover Austrian companies, how do you know which company they matched? There is no worldwide unique company identifier.

And if you do it yourself: how do you know that this website really belongs to this company? You have to validate every single match (e. g. through the imprint on a company's website in Austria).

There are quite a few more challenges involved, but we're happy with where this first, admittedly small, result has landed. Feedback very welcome – especially on which relationships would make a graph like this useful for you.

Feedback welcome!

Hi Folks, Having been on the applicant side of hiring late, I've notice a lot of similar posts from people in the same situation (frequency illusion ?), due to the volume of applications they are unsure their CV is reviewed by human eyes.

Separately, I've started reaching out to hiring managers, recruiters, agencies etc to get their input. There has been a common thread in their response, AI is used to review and "grade" submissions but its not uncommon for lower graded submissions to actually get the job over higher graded submissions.

A few are using off the shelf software, others have created their own harness. We are seemingly in the world of applicants using AI to help apply, and AI grading the submissions. With Pandora's box opened, it's difficult to see AI ever being completely removed from the process, but it feels like a vicious cycle.

(Job Market is tough -> People using AI to apply (sometimes auto apply) to jobs with targeted, enhanced or fabricated CVs -> Job openings receiving increased and overwhelming number of applications -> using AI to help filter and reduce the noise -> repeat).

For people hiring, are you seeing the same? Do CV's carry the same weight as they use to and are screen calls now a necessary requirement? For people applying, how often are getting feedback & are far are you tailoring your CV?

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I made git-dupe to solve the problem where I have notes, skills, and agent instructions that are part of my personal workflow, so I do not want them committed to the public repo, but at the same time, I want them to be in the project at the correct locations (e.g., AGENTS.md file locations matter), and these files cannot be simply gitignored because I want versioning for them.

The solution that I've come upon is versioning those agent files in another repo, say <private-repo> (this repo is private to me and holds the history for my agent files). The project itself is open to the public in another <public-repo>. I overlap the two repos to solve the problem (i.e., they share the same worktree).

  $ git status --short              # the public repo
  ?? AGENTS.md
  ?? notes/

  $ git dupe init                   # the private repo
  Initialized empty Git repository in /home/brian/code/project/.git/dupe/

  $ git dupe add notes/ AGENTS.md   # the private repo
  hint: notes is now hidden from the project's Git; run from the root, 'git dupe unhide -- notes' stops hiding it

  $ git dupe commit -m "Notes and agent instructions"        # the private repo
  [main (root-commit) 3eb3af9] Notes and agent instructions
   3 files changed, 3 insertions(+)
   create mode 100644 .gitdupe
   create mode 100644 AGENTS.md
   create mode 100644 notes/todo.md

  $ git status --short              # the public repo: nothing

  $ git dupe log --oneline          # the private repo: your files
  3eb3af9 Notes and agent instructions
In short, git-dupe allows two Git repos to share the same worktree, while using native Git for most operations. Most git-dupe commands behave just like normal Git commands, operating on the private repo instead.

git-dupe currently supports Linux and macOS, and is under the MIT License; the git-dupe repo contains much more extensive technical documentation documentation for those who are interested. If you have any feedback/questions about git-dupe, feel free to message. I hope it helps!

Fun fact: the git-dupe project itself is using git-dupe for versioning.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Alexander. Yes, this is another agent harness. Here is why I built one anyway.

I was engineer #2 at Browser Use, where I built our agent harness and the evals behind it, including BU Bench, which became a default benchmark for browser agents. I left in September to build Mainplane.

The problem: local agents die with your laptop, and cloud agents can't reach your work. Many cloud platforms ask you to "select a repository", but my work is not that simple. I work across a desktop, a Mac mini and a laptop, and much of it is not in git.

So I loaded Ubuntu on my old 2012 desktop and made it my Mainplane server. It has run for four weeks at a load average of 0.02, because the agents' tools run on other machines.

How it works: it is a control plane architecture. The server runs the harness. It holds your API keys and every session, makes the LLM calls, and routes each tool call to a worker. The workers are your other machines, connected over a built-in private WireGuard network. A bash command runs in the worker's terminal, not on the server. Shared drives let projects move across machines. The agent works on your machines just like you would, but its state lives on the server, and your keys never leave it.

Some design choices:

- Every session is one append-only file. This is the agent state, and it is easily readable. If something breaks, you can resume it from the file. Observability comes for free: agent traces are just these state files.

- Small by design. The system prompt is 3k tokens, and there are just two kinds of tools: shell and file (read, write, edit). At Browser Use, I learned the bitter lesson and found frontier models did better when I deleted all our helper functions. So I made the same bet here: bash is all you need.

- No compaction. When a session fills up, /continue starts a new one that greps the previous state file, retrieving the context it needs, instead of reading a lossy summary. A /compact on a 400k-token session takes a while to write its summary. A /continue into a brand new session starts at once.

- No permission prompts. A hyperintelligent misaligned agent WILL find a way around a permission system. The better strategy is giving the agent full unbounded access to a local computer, and only putting what you trust the agent with on that computer.

- Why Go. WireGuard is written in Go, so the network compiles right into a 20 MB binary. Go is made for production servers, LLMs write it well, and the simplicity of Go matches how I like to build.

Mainplane works with a Claude or ChatGPT subscription on the regular usage limits, or any API key.

I would love your feedback, especially brutal and honest feedback and tasks that the harness cannot do. I'll be here all day to answer questions.

story_text.value:
This is hardly a greenfield area. There are tons of agent-to-agent communication apps. But, at least to my taste, a lot of them are too complicated or too opinionated. If we learned anything from the HuggingFace incident, it's that modern AI agents don't need a lot of help communicating. They are smart and creative and figure it out.

So...with that in mind, I (meaning I + claude and friends) built kashkeshet, or kkt. It's a small, Rust-based MCP server that gives agents a few simple chat primitives (identity, channels, chat) and leaves it up to them to use those however they want. You as the human get a little web interface so you can watch the fun.

Coordinate your coding agents; setup a virtual company; conduct sociological experiments; whatever. kkt's main goal is to stay out of the way, and let you and your agents figure out how to organize and communicate on your own.

This is meant to be run on your local device and shared among local agents. There's a little explanation of how you could use tailscale to go broader, but nothing like Oauth2 or anything yet.

Hello HN!

As someone who would have otherwise never got into game development if it wasn't for AI, I'm really sorry to see how many peoples' creations get immediately overlooked because it's "AI slop." Slop or not, many people have very interesting and/or original concepts, and regardless of the means of production I believe there should be a place for someone to at least enjoy.

And that's why I made this directory. Yes, I know it gets to the XKCD 927 situation, but I haven't heard of any other platform for these "Claudeslop" games. So here we go!

This is basically the doomgeneric idea but applied to Minecraft (its first version rd-132211 that came out on 13 May 2009).

It's one freestanding C file with no includes and no memory allocation. It runs in a terminal, over telnet as shared multiplayer, as a 20 KB wasm module, inside a PDF on Chrome and on a bare x86 PC with no OS, and on a jailbroken Kindle Paperwhite.

PDFium doesn't have WebAssembly so the C goes to wasm with clang and then binaryen's wasm2js turns it into JavaScript.

It also compiles for a Raspberry Pi Pico and Game Boy Advance, but I don't have any of these so haven't tested it. If someone has one would love to hear how it works there. The browser version can be played here directly: https://pragyaangaur.github.io/Can-It-Run-Minecraft

Used Claude for the C and JavaScript code because that's outside my area of work. I picked the targets and tested everything. The Kindle version ended up being an extended project so it's not in the linked repo: https://github.com/pragyaangaur/Inkwell

And if anyone has any crazier places it could run on (someone please do it on a pregnancy test) do try and share it... maybe I could add it to the repo!

I built something for someone who needed a website, but didn't want to be exposed to yet another complicated CMS like WordPress. They already use Google Docs, so I built Foldocs for them to publish and maintain a simple website.

Foldocs creates static HTML pages out of a (shared) folder of documents in Google Drive (or Nextcloud!): (sub)folders become (sub)sections on the site, and documents inside them become pages. Does it work? Proof is to be found in the pudding: Foldocs.com, the site that explains Foldocs, is itself a Foldocs site! The underlying Google Drive is here: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1ZRYhiIGfSeIcA_gjRVgT....

Foldocs is an open source (AGPL 3.0) Python engine anyone can run. It currently supports three themes, dark mode, and an RSS feed. You can also try it out by creating a preview on https://try.foldocs.com. Paste a shared folder link, and see a preview (kept for 7 days, limited in files / size, and only syncs manually). Previews are running on a separate domain and a throwaway VPS, since hosting strangers' content on the internet is... scary.

Curious to hear what you think of the concept, learn what breaks (but don't try too hard please), what you run into, and/or what is missing!

story_text.value:
I built Formstep: https://formstep.io

The idea came from a problem I kept running into while working on loan applications.

A workflow could automate a large part of the process, but eventually it would need something only the customer could provide: a document, a correction, a signature, an explanation, or confirmation of some information.

At that point, workflow automation basically did not work.

The forms themselves were also often the source of the problem. Applications came in with wrong documents, misunderstood questions, incomplete answers, or people simply forgetting to finish.

Someone had to email the customer, explain what was missing, wait for a reply then follow up again. It was always back-and-forth.

So I built Formstep to make requesting information from customers easier, not only for humans, but also for workflows and AI agents.

The idea is: A person, workflow, or AI agent sends a customer a request through email or a link. Either re-use existing form or create unique for each customer.

You can prefill what you already know, lock fields, pass context, and only ask the customer what you need.

For example, we might already know:

* Address that you already have in the CRM

* Company description from the internet

* What a agreement document must contain

* How a good answer should be

Formstep can check inputs and uploaded files while the customer is filling out the form and tell them if something is missing or inconsistent before they submit. For example “The PDF does not contain your signature” or “Invoice total does not match the order amount”.

The goal is to catch problems while the customer is still there, rather than letting bad data continue through the workflow and discovering it later.

On the automation side, requests can currently be created through n8n, Zapier, the REST API, or by an AI agent over MCP. When the customer finishes, the structured answers can go back into the workflow so it can continue.

Forms and invitation/reminder are multilingual, and submitted answers can be translated inside the dashboard with one click. If you want, Formstep can be used as normal form builder and shared through public links, QR, embeds etc. It support custom themes for dark/light mode, with cover image, has Notion-style editor and much more. The list is too long to fit here.

I want to make Formstep a plattform where it becomes more intelligent over time and ensures that we can get better answers from customers for any use case.

My question to you: Where do your automations currently stop because they need input from a customer or user, and how are you handling that today?

If you are interested in trying out the n8n node: https://www.npmjs.com/package/n8n-nodes-formstep

Zapier integration: https://zapier.com/apps/formstep/integrations

Connecting your AI agent: https://docs.formstep.io/developers/mcp-server/

Docs: https://docs.formstep.io

I would love your feedback and please try a quick demo at https://app.formstep.io/try

story_text.value:
I used GameMaker 8.1 a ton in late elementary and middle school, and GML was the first programming language I wrote. I still think it's a fun engine to use because it has so many batteries included. So I built an open-source reimplementation of it in Rust which I'm calling Instance. It opens existing .gmk and .gm81 projects and runs them on Windows, macOS and in the browser, with a more efficient GML interpreter than the original GameMaker.

You can try the IDE here in your browser: https://groverburger.github.io/instance/. It comes with three example games, including Spelunky Classic built from Derek Yu's released source shared under its permissive license. Just change something and press Run to see your edits in action.

Old GM games depend on a lot of quirks such as the order events run in, the exact random number generator, how sound_isplaying lags behind the audio. I wrote up the behavior as specs from the documentation, the file formats and black-box tests against the real program, then implemented it from those specs. No proprietary code was disassembled or decompiled. CLEANROOM.md describes the process.

It covers most of almost all of 8.1. All the resource editors, GML and drag-and-drop actions, d3d, particles, surfaces, MIDI, mplay multiplayer and DLL calls. It can also export a game as a standalone executable or a single HTML file. Projects can be saved as folders of plain text and PNG files for git.

I wrote most of the code with Claude Opus 5.5 over about three weeks. Claude banged out a pretty good reimplementation in a morning, but as always the last 20% took 80% of the work. GameMaker also turns out to work surprisingly well with LLMs. GML is small and simple, and a whole game fits in one project file.

I'm happy to answer any questions!

Code: https://github.com/groverburger/instance
